summary: This is an April 1st joke RFC that adapts RFC 1149, which describes sending IP datagrams by carrier pigeon, to IPv6. It is humorous, not a real protocol, though it is written in the style of a serious one.

eli5.summary: Someone wrote a joke rule book for sending internet messages by pigeon, and this one updates it for newer addresses. Nobody is expected to do it for real.

questions: is there an rfc for carrier pigeons
how big is the mtu for avian carriers
subtitle: An April 1st joke spec for sending IPv6 packets by carrier pigeon, updating RFC 1149.

tldr.problem: Service providers that already run IP over avian carriers (RFC 1149) face the shortage of IPv4 addresses and the move to IPv6, and the joke says they should not have to change medium.
tldr.mechanism: It carries a pure IPv6 packet with no link layer tag over the RFC 1149 medium, and works through MTU, addressing, multicast, QoS, routing and multihoming as they apply to birds.
tldr.outcome: It is an April 1st humor document, published for information only and not a candidate for any Internet Standard.

today: RFC 6214 is an April 1st Informational document that updates RFC 1149 and has not been obsoleted. It is humor and not a candidate for any Internet Standard.

sections.title: The Joke: IPv6 by Pigeon
sections.content:
RFC 6214 is an April 1st joke document, dated 1 April 2011. It updates RFC 1149, the earlier joke spec for carrying IP datagrams on avian carriers. It is written in the deadpan style of a real specification.

The introduction argues, citing RFC 6036, that many service providers are planning to deploy IPv6. It calls it urgent to specify IPv6 over the RFC 1149 medium, so that those providers need not move to a different medium. Unless otherwise stated, the rules of RFC 1149 and RFC 2460 apply.
sections.eli5: Pigeon mail already had a joke rule book. This one says how to send the newer kind of internet message the same way.

sections.title: Carrier Age, MTU and Frame Format
sections.content:
RFC 1149 has a variable MTU that grows with carrier age. Since RFC 2460 sets a minimum link MTU of 1280 octets, older carriers MUST be used for IPv6. As an illustrative example only, the text assumes the 256 milligram MTU of RFC 1149 equals 576 octets, which gives at least about 569 milligrams and a carrier age of at least 365 days. The effect is non-linear: young carriers carry small payloads, adults can carry jumbograms, and elderly carriers again carry less.

No link layer tag is used, since header snaps are said to worsen service. The frame is a pure IPv6 packet. In a dual-stack deployment the receiver MUST inspect the version number in the first four bits of every packet to tell IPv4 from IPv6.
sections.eli5: Bigger messages need an older, stronger bird. Very young birds and very old birds can only carry small ones.

sections.title: Addresses, Multicast and Service Classes
sections.content:
With no link layer there are no link-local addresses, no way to map an IPv6 address to a link address, and so Neighbor Discovery is impossible. Implementations SHOULD NOT try stateless address autoconfiguration (RFC 4862), because carriers are not stable enough, especially in a cross-wind. Endpoints stay unnumbered, or a /127 prefix and static addresses MAY be used. No IPv6 multicast mapping is specified, because IPv4 multicast attempts reportedly caused excessive noise.

For quality of service, RFC 2549 also applies. Packets with a non-default DSCP MUST be marked in green or blue ink, and red ink MUST NOT be used, to avoid confusion with the red paint of RFC 2549. Different carriers may suit different DSCP values.
sections.eli5: Pigeons have no street names, so you just point them at the other end. Special mail gets marked with green or blue ink, never red.

sections.title: Routing, Multihoming and Safety
sections.content:
Routing carriers through the territory of similar carriers without peering agreements may cause route changes, loops and out-of-order delivery, and predatory carriers may cause severe packet loss. The RFC suggests policy-based routing around such areas. It also muses that carriers eating other carriers could be a way to tunnel IPv4 in IPv6, though the decapsulation mechanism is unclear.

Homing carriers have no talent for multihoming and enter a routing loop when it is tried. The security section says the RFC 1149 considerations apply, that transmission elements are exposed to denial-of-service attacks especially when perching, and that an upper-layer security mechanism seems like a really good idea. Appropriate detection and quarantine measures for H5N1 MUST be available. IANA is asked to do nothing.
sections.eli5: Hungry hawks can eat your pigeons, and homing pigeons only want to go home. So keep messages safe and do not expect two homes to work.
